keyTerms.definition: A precise statement of what you want to find out; an experiment can answer it.
What you are studying; one of four parts with comparison, measure, scope.
The part most questions skip: how will you tell the difference.
The boundary of your claim; state it now.

recall.question: What are the four parts of a good research question?
Why does 'Make transformers better' fail?
recall.answer: It has none of the four parts.

sections.title: 2. How to read a paper: the 3-pass method

keyTerms.definition: How to read a paper before running a single experiment.
The next problem after the question: absorb what others found.

recall.question: Why read before experimenting?
recall.answer: To absorb what others found; skipping means repeating work.

sections.title: 3. Literature review: mapping the field before you contribute

keyTerms.definition: A systematic map of prior work; find the blank space your question fills.
The one-paragraph gap your work will fill.

recall.question: What are the two scale questions?
recall.answer: How to turn fifty papers into a map, and how to find the blank space.

keyTerms.definition: A falsifiable prediction: 'If X, then Y, because Z.'
The rival: the boring alternative that the change does nothing.

recall.question: Why state the hypothesis before touching data?
recall.answer: So the experiment can surprise you instead of confirming what you hoped.

recall.question: Why design to disprove the null?
recall.answer: Not to confirm your belief; without the mechanism a correct prediction is luck.

sections.title: 5. Designing experiments: ablations that prove something

keyTerms.definition: One row per component, one edit per row; change two things and you prove nothing.
Asks whether the sophistication was needed at all.

recall.question: What makes a good ablation table?
recall.answer: One row per component, one edit per row; the full method is the reference row to beat.

keyTerms.definition: Compute, tuning, data, seeds; interrogate every win with the boring explanation first.
What to do with ideas that fail.

recall.question: What is the confounder pattern?
recall.answer: Hold the confounder fixed and re-run; a result surviving all four is worth believing.

keyTerms.definition: Probability of seeing this difference if nothing were really there.
The honest range around your measurement.
Makes small-sample ML comparisons honest.

recall.question: What does 'significant' mean?
recall.answer: Unlikely to have arisen by chance alone; nothing more.

keyTerms.definition: Exact claim, method, full evidence, interpretation labeled as yours.
Carries numbers and conditions.

recall.question: What makes a results writeup trusted?
recall.answer: Four load-bearing parts including the negative results found along the way.

keyTerms.definition: Fixes the story before the data: hypothesis, metric, seeds, analysis plan.
Layers: re-runnable, replicable, robust, preregistered.

recall.question: What are the two remaining problems?
recall.answer: Will it hold in six months, and was the story fixed before the data arrived.

sections.title: 10. Research taste: choosing what to work on

keyTerms.definition: Three filters: importance, tractability, neglect.
Is nobody doing this from a real barrier or just inattention.

recall.question: What are the three filters?
recall.answer: Importance, tractability, neglect; fail ideas fast, in days not months.

sections.title: 11. Capstone: replicate a result on your own compute

keyTerms.definition: A published result on your own compute, end to end.
Questions, reading, hypotheses, ablations, statistics, writeups, reproducibility.

recall.question: What does the capstone answer?
recall.answer: Whether you can use the toolkit: replicate a result on your own compute.

keyTerms.definition: 'You and Your Research': choosing problems worth solving; companion to chapter 10.
Eight questions every research proposal should answer.

recall.question: Which talk companions chapter 8?
recall.answer: Simon Peyton Jones on structuring a paper so readers trust it.
